summary: Describes the "environment" extension to the Sieve filtering language. It gives a script access to information about the Sieve interpreter itself, where it is running, and the transport connection used to deliver the message. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: This lets an email filter ask about its own surroundings, like what program am I and where am I running, so rules can adapt.

questions: what is the sieve environment extension
what environment items does sieve define
how do i register a sieve environment item
can i trust the sieve remote-host item
subtitle: A Sieve extension that lets an email filter script ask about the system it is running on.

tldr.problem: Sieve scripts are meant to be independent of mail architecture and operating system, but sometimes a script needs to know where and how it is running, for example to behave differently on another system.
tldr.mechanism: The "environment" extension adds an environment test that looks up a named item, such as host, location or remote-ip, and matches it against a list of keys supplied by the script.
tldr.outcome: Scripts can adapt to the system, the point of delivery and the connecting client, and new items can be added through an IANA registry.

today: RFC 5183 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Filter Needs Its Surroundings
sections.content:
Sieve (RFC 5228) is a language for filtering email messages at or around the time of final delivery. It can run on a mail client or a mail server, and it has no user-controlled loops and cannot run external programs, which makes it suitable for servers where users may not run arbitrary programs.

Sieve is meant to be independent of access protocol, mail architecture and operating system. Even so, it is sometimes useful for a script to learn about its execution context. The environment extension adds a new environment test for scripts that behave differently when moved from one system to another, when messages arrive from different remote sources, or when operated in different contexts. Its capability string is environment.
sections.eli5: An email filter normally only looks at the letter. This extension lets it also look around and ask where it is and who handed it the letter.

sections.title: The environment Test
sections.content:
The usage is environment [COMPARATOR] [MATCH-TYPE] <name: string> <key-list: string-list>. The test retrieves the environment item called name and matches it against the values in the key list. It succeeds if a match occurs. The match type defaults to :is and the default comparator is i;ascii-casemap.

The current message is not a source for this test. The item comes from the script's operating environment, and the keys come from the script.

If the named item does not exist, the test MUST fail unconditionally, and a script MUST NOT fail with an error. That lets scripts handle missing items gracefully. A side effect is that environment :contains "item" "" succeeds only if the implementation knows the item, and always succeeds if it does.

With the relational extension (RFC 5231), the :count of an environment test is 0 if the returned information is the empty string, and 1 otherwise.
sections.eli5: The script says the name of something it wants to know and a list of answers it would accept. If the real answer is on the list, the rule fires. If the question makes no sense to the system, the answer is just no.

sections.title: The Initial Standard Items
sections.content:
The RFC defines an initial set of standardized items. Implementations SHOULD support as many as possible.

  • domain: the primary DNS domain of the Sieve execution context, usually but not always a proper suffix of the host name.
  • host: the fully-qualified domain name of the host running the script.
  • location: the kind of service evaluating the script. Values are MTA (Message Transfer Agent), MDA (Mail Delivery Agent), MUA (Mail User Agent) and MS (Message Store).
  • name and version: the product name and version of the Sieve interpreter. The version string only makes sense together with the name.
  • phase: the point relative to final delivery, one of pre, during or post.
  • remote-host: the host name of the remote SMTP, LMTP or Submission client as an FQDN, if applicable and available. It is the empty string if the information cannot be obtained.
  • remote-ip: the IP address of that client, if applicable and available, written as an IPv4, IPv6 or general address literal as defined in RFC 2821.
sections.eli5: It is like a name tag with blanks: which computer I am on, what kind of mail worker I am, whether the letter is before or after delivery, and who sent it to me.

sections.title: Vendor Items and the IANA Registry
sections.content:
Environment items can be standardized or vendor-defined, and IANA keeps a registry for both. Names are registered on a first-come, first-served basis. Items defined in a standards track or experimental RFC may share a common prefix of the form name. for a group of related items. Additional standardized items can only be defined in standards-track or experimental RFCs.

Items not defined in such an RFC MUST begin with the vnd. prefix followed by the vendor or product name, for example vnd.acme.rocket-sled-status. They are not Internet standards, but are registered to prevent conflicts. The RFC gives an email template for registrations with an item name, a description, an RFC number and a contact address.
sections.eli5: Anyone can add a new question to the list, but company-made questions must start with a special label so they never clash with the official ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension can be used to obtain information about the system the Sieve implementation is running on, which in turn may reveal details about service provider or enterprise infrastructure.

The remote-host item can be determined by any technique, and the result is only as trustworthy as that technique. A common method is a PTR DNS lookup on the client IP address, which may come from an untrusted source. The RFC warns that environment :matches "remote-host" "*.example.com" is not a good way to tell whether a message came from outside, because anyone who can create a PTR record can make it point to any domain. All security considerations of the base Sieve specification also apply.
sections.eli5: A name found by looking up a number can be faked by whoever controls that entry, so do not trust it like an ID card.
